About Jack

I’m Jackson. I live in Singapore, I have a day job and a toddler, and I write about the Pokémon TCG in the hours that are left over.

ItemSixHQ is where all of that lives — the guides, the tools, the news write-ups, and my own binder. It’s one person, working at night. There is no company behind it and nobody pays me to do it.

I write mainly for players in Singapore and the wider region, because almost everything written about this game in English is written for somewhere else.

YouTube TikTok Telegram

What I make

  • A beginners guide and an advanced guide — free, fact-checked against official rulings, written for someone who has never played a card game.
  • A rotation checker — paste a decklist, find out what’s about to stop being legal. Free, no sign-up, nothing stored.
  • Ask Jack — the questions I actually get asked, answered honestly, including the ones where the answer is “don’t buy it”.
  • News write-ups in my own words rather than reposted press releases.
  • A running guide to Worlds 2027 for anyone travelling to Singapore for it.

Why I write for this part of the world

Nearly all English-language Pokémon TCG coverage is made in North America. That’s not a complaint — it’s just where the audience has been. But it means a player in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia or the Philippines reads guides where the prices are in the wrong currency, the shops are on the wrong continent, the release dates don’t match, and the advice about “your local league” assumes a scene that works nothing like ours.

In August 2027 the World Championships come to Singapore. For a lot of players in this region it will be the first time the biggest event in the game has been anywhere they could realistically get to.

I’d like the English-language guide to that to come from someone who actually lives here.

The rest of it

I’m a singer-songwriter, and I manage operations at a music school. I’m a husband and a dad to a toddler. Those aren’t things I do instead of this — they’re why the writing here is the way it is. I don’t have time to pad anything out, and I have no interest in selling anyone something they don’t need.

It also means I’m honest about pace. This isn’t a full-time operation and I’m not going to pretend otherwise.

The binder

Everything in the binder is mine, described the way I’d want it described to me, and priced off what cards have actually sold for. I’m happy to trade or to sell, and there’s no checkout — every one of those ends up as a conversation.

Giving Back

Free draws going out, spare cards coming in. Neither one involves money.

Giveaways and lucky draws

I haven’t nailed down exactly how this will run yet, but the idea is simple: give cards away to people in the Singapore Pokémon community, particularly the ones just starting out.

Always free to enter. Entry will never cost anything, and will never require buying a card or spending money with me — that’s a promise, not a current limitation. If you ever see a draw claiming to be mine that asks you to purchase something first, it isn’t mine.

Nothing running right now. It’ll be announced here and on Telegram when there is.

Donating cards to me

If you’ve got English cards you’d rather pass on than bin, I’ll take them. They either go into the binder or get handed to someone learning the game — usually the second one, because a beginner holding a real deck does more for this hobby than another card in my folder.

Cards only. I don’t accept money here, and there’s nothing on this site that would let you send any. Given freely, no strings, nothing expected in return — and no obligation on your side either.

Non-bulk English cards are the useful ones. If you’re not sure whether something counts, just ask me.

New to the Pokémon TCG? Start Here.

I get asked “how do I even start playing” more than anything else — way more than card values, honestly. So here it is: everything you need to sit down with a friend and play a full game, assuming you know nothing. This is the paper game, though Pokémon TCG Live works the same way. Once it clicks, the Advanced Guide takes it further.

The goal

You win one of three ways:

Take all your Prize cards. You set aside 6 face-down at the start. Knock out one of your opponent’s Pokémon and you take Prizes for it:

  • A regular Pokémon — 1 Prize
  • An ex Pokémon — 2 Prizes
  • A Mega Pokémon — 3 Prizes

Your opponent runs out of Pokémon. No Pokémon in play, none left to play — game over.

Your opponent can’t draw a card. If someone’s deck is empty on their draw step, they lose right there. This is also called “decking your opponent out” — it barely ever comes up in a casual game, but it’s a real strategy some decks are built entirely around. If you’re familiar with other TCGs, the term is also called milling.

Most games end this way. The thing to hold onto: the bigger and splashier the Pokémon, the more it hands your opponent when it goes down.

What’s in a deck

60 cards, always. Three types: Pokémon cards — what you actually play and attack with. Trainer cards — Items, Supporters, Stadiums, and Tools, doing everything from drawing extra cards to searching your deck to healing damage. Energy cards — attach these to power up your Pokémon’s attacks.

Here’s what each one actually looks like:

AlakazamPokémon card
Poké PadItem card
Lillie’s DeterminationSupporter card
Battle CageStadium card
Handheld FanTool card

You can only run 4 copies of any card with the same name (max 4 Pikachu, max 4 Ultra Ball, etc.) — the one exception is basic Energy, which you can run as many of as you want. There are 8 basic Energy types, and there’s no dedicated Colourless Energy card — Colourless costs in attacks can be paid with any Energy type:

That unlimited-copies rule only applies to plain basic Energy — cards with no text on them beyond their name and type. Special Energy cards (Mist Energy, Bubbly Energy, and the like) do have an effect printed on them, so they’re treated like any other card and capped at the normal 4 copies.

Grass
Fire
Water
Lightning
Psychic
Fighting
Dark
Steel

Setting up

Before a game starts, players usually give each other a friendly fist bump — a small sign of respect. It’s not an official rule and nobody will stop you skipping it. But do skip it, and you’ll be the only one who did.

Shuffle your deck. The general rule is to always offer your deck to your opponent to “cut” every time you shuffle it — it’s entirely up to them whether they want to.

Draw 7 cards. You need at least one Basic Pokémon somewhere in that hand. If you don’t have one, that’s a mulligan: reveal your hand to your opponent to prove it, shuffle it back into your deck, and draw a fresh 7. Keep doing this until you draw a Basic. Once both hands are set up, your opponent gets to draw one extra card for every mulligan you took — unless they also had to mulligan, in which case it cancels out and nobody draws extra.

Set a Basic Pokémon face-down as your Active Pokémon (the one doing the fighting) — you can also place more Basics face-down on your Bench, up to 5. Once both players are ready, flip everything face-up, set aside your 6 Prize cards, and you’re in.

Whoever goes first is decided however you like — coin flip, rock-paper-scissors, doesn’t matter.

How a turn works

Every turn has three parts, always in this order:

1. Draw. Draw one card. Mandatory, no skipping it.

2. Main phase. As much or as little of this as you like, in any order:

  • Play Basic Pokémon to your Bench (5 max)
  • Evolve a Pokémon
  • Attach one Energy from your hand — one per turn total, not one per Pokémon
  • Use Pokémon Abilities
  • Play any number of Item cards
  • Play one Supporter and one Stadium
  • Retreat your Active Pokémon once, paying its Retreat Cost

3. Attack. Pick an attack your Active Pokémon has enough Energy for, resolve it, and your turn ends. One attack per turn, and once you attack, that’s it.

Turn 1 is different

Read this before your first game.

This is the part that confuses almost every new player, so here it is on its own:

If you go first: your very first turn only, you draw as normal, but you cannot attack and cannot play a Supporter card. Everything else in the main phase is still fair game — playing Basics, attaching Energy, using Abilities, playing Items or a Stadium, retreating. In practice, this just means turn 1 for the first player is: set up your board and pass.

If you go second: none of that applies to you. Despite it also being your first turn, you play a completely normal turn — full main phase, and yes, you can attack.

From turn 2 onward, both players play full, unrestricted turns.

Evolution, explained

Basics evolve into Stage 1s, and some Stage 1s evolve again into Stage 2s — follow the chain printed on the card. Place the new card directly on top of the old one. It keeps everything already attached: Energy, damage, Tools. It’s the same Pokémon, just bigger.

The timing rule: a Pokémon has to have been in play since the start of your turn. Two consequences — you can’t evolve something the turn you play it, and nobody evolves anything on turn 1.

Each Pokémon evolves once per turn (no Basic → Stage 1 → Stage 2 in one go), but you can evolve as many different Pokémon in a turn as you like.

Some cards deliberately break this rule — Rare Candy, and Stadiums like Forest of Vitality. That’s covered in the Advanced Guide.

What’s next

That’s genuinely enough to sit down and play a full game.

When the basics start feeling automatic, the Advanced Guide picks up from here — status conditions, rotation and regulation marks, prize mapping, sequencing, and what to expect at your first tournament.

Otherwise: Meta Decks for what’s winning, Jack’s Decks for what I play, or Play with Jack if you fancy a game.

Advanced Guide

Finished the Beginners Guide and want the next layer? This is the stuff that turns “I can play a game” into “I know what I’m doing.”

None of this is needed to sit down and play. It matters when you start caring about winning — or when you start buying cards for a tournament deck rather than for the binder. Work through it in order, or jump to whatever you’re stuck on.

  • Special Conditions — the five status effects, and what actually removes them
  • Evolution: the exceptions — Rare Candy, Stadiums that break the rule
  • Standard format and rotation — regulation marks, and what’s legal
  • ACE SPEC cards — the one-per-deck rule
  • Prize mapping — planning your six knockouts before you take the first
  • Sequencing — playing the right card first
  • Your first tournament — deck lists, deck checks, sleeves

Special Conditions

Five status effects exist. They only ever apply to the Active Pokémon — the moment a Pokémon goes to the Bench, every Special Condition on it disappears. That’s the single most useful thing to remember here: retreating is a cure.

Three of them are shown by physically turning the card, and because a card can only face one direction at a time, only one of those three can be on a Pokémon at once — a new one replaces the old. The other two use damage-counter-style markers, so they can sit alongside anything.

Asleep
Can’t attack or retreat. At Pokémon Checkup, flip a coin — heads and it wakes up. Card is turned counter-clockwise.
Paralyzed
Can’t attack or retreat. Clears automatically at the start of that player’s next turn, so it only ever costs one turn. Card is turned clockwise.
Confused
Can still retreat, but to attack you flip a coin first — tails and the attack fails, 3 damage counters go on your own Pokémon, and your turn ends. Card is turned upside-down.
Burned
At Checkup, put 2 damage counters on it, then flip a coin — heads removes the Burn, tails and it stays. Uses a marker.
Poisoned
At Checkup, put 1 damage counter on it (some cards make it more). Nothing removes it on its own — you retreat, evolve, or play a card that clears it. Uses a marker.

Pokémon Checkup is the little step between turns where Burn and Poison damage lands and Sleep coins get flipped. New players routinely forget it exists; it’s a genuinely common way to lose a game you should have won.

Two more things worth knowing: evolving a Pokémon clears its Special Conditions too, and Burned and Poisoned can both be on the same Pokémon at the same time as one of the turned-card conditions. So a Pokémon can be Asleep, Burned and Poisoned at once — it just can’t be Asleep and Paralyzed at once.

Evolution: the exceptions

The Beginners Guide gives you the normal rule: a Pokémon has to have been in play since the start of your turn, so you can’t evolve something the turn you played it, and nobody evolves anything on turn 1.

That’s the default. Cards are allowed to override it, and some do:

  • Rare Candy skips the middle step entirely — it takes a Basic straight to a Stage 2. It still can’t be used on a Pokémon you put into play that same turn.
  • Forest of Vitality (Stadium, Mega Evolution 117 — also reprinted in Ascended Heroes and Perfect Order) reads: “Each player’s Grass Pokémon can evolve into Grass Pokémon during the turn they play those Pokémon, except during their first turn.” So a Grass deck running this can play a Basic and evolve it immediately — but not on turn 1, and it doesn’t let Rare Candy break its own rule either. Note it says each player’s: your opponent gets the same benefit while it’s on the field.

The general principle: a specific card beats the general rule. If a card says it can do something the rulebook says you can’t, the card wins. That’s true across the whole game, not just evolution.

Rotation and regulation marks

If you’re buying singles or building a tournament-legal deck, you need to know about rotation. Every card released has a small letter printed on it — the regulation mark — usually near the artist credit or set symbol. Once a year, the oldest regulation marks get rotated out of the Standard format, so the format keeps refreshing instead of accumulating years of cards.

The current rotation took effect this year — regulation mark G and everything older is no longer Standard-legal, and only cards marked H, I, and J are tournament-legal in Standard right now. Practically, that means anything from Twilight Masquerade onward is safe to build around, and anything from the original Scarlet & Violet base set through Paradox Rift just rotated out. New sets keep adding new regulation marks as they release, and each stays legal until it’s old enough to rotate out in turn.

Here’s exactly what that mark looks like on two real cards from my own binder — a small letter in a box, bottom-left, near the illustrator credit:

Regulation mark H — e.g. Dudunsparce (Prismatic Evolutions)

Regulation mark J — e.g. Mega Chandelure ex

Keep this in mind if you’re investing in Standard-legal cards: regulation mark H is the oldest of the three currently legal, and following the usual annual pattern, it’s expected to rotate out around April next year. Once that happens, only I and J (plus whatever’s newest by then) will remain Standard-legal.

One more wrinkle: legality is tracked per printing, not per card name. A lot of Trainer and Pokémon cards get reprinted — sometimes with the exact same art, sometimes with a new one — in later sets. If a card you own has an old, rotated-out mark, but that same card (by name and effect) later gets reprinted under a current mark like H, I, or J, only that new printing is tournament-legal. Your older-art copy with the old mark still isn’t legal, even though it’s technically “the same card.” So don’t go by whether the card has been reprinted somewhere — check the actual regulation mark on the specific copy you own.

If you’re just playing casually with friends, none of this matters — play with whatever cards you own. It only bites you if you’re building for an actual Standard tournament.

ACE SPEC cards

Some Trainer and Energy cards carry an ACE SPEC banner running diagonally down the side. Whatever it is — Item, Tool, or Energy — you can only run one ACE SPEC card in your entire deck, on top of the normal 4-copy limit. They exist because the effect is usually strong enough that the format wouldn’t be balanced without that cap.

On rotation: ACE SPEC isn’t its own block that rotates all at once — each ACE SPEC card rotates exactly like any other card, based on the regulation mark printed on it. The three below are all marked H, so if H rotates out around April next year as expected (see above), these three specific cards go with it — but newer ACE SPECs printed under I, J, or later marks won’t be affected by that.

Precious TrolleyItem · ACE SPEC
Legacy EnergyEnergy · ACE SPEC
Hero’s CapeTool · ACE SPEC

Prize mapping

You need six Prizes to win. Different Pokémon are worth different amounts — a regular Pokémon is 1, an ex is 2, a Mega is 3. Prize mapping is just working out, in advance, which knockouts add up to six.

Do the maths before you attack, not after. A few common shapes:

  • 2–2–2 — three knockouts on two-Prize Pokémon and the game’s over. The cleanest map, and the one most decks are built around.
  • 1–1–2–2 — pick off two small Pokémon first, then take two big ones. Slower, but it lets you attack whatever’s actually in front of you.
  • 3–3 — two Mega knockouts. Rare, but it happens.

The reason this matters: it changes what you attack. If knocking out the big threat in front of you puts your opponent on exactly six, and you could instead knock out something small and set up a clean two-turn finish, the small one is often the right play. Deciding that mid-attack is how games get lost.

The flip side is the prize trade — what your opponent gets back. Attacking with a one-Prize Pokémon into their two-Prize one is a good trade even if it takes an extra turn, because when they knock you out they only get one back.

Sequencing

Same cards, same turn, different order — different outcome. That’s sequencing, and it’s probably the single biggest gap between a casual player and a good one.

Three rules of thumb cover most of it:

  • Draw before you search. Play your draw Supporter first, then your Ultra Ball. Once you’ve seen the extra cards you know what you actually need — searching first means guessing.
  • Commit last. Attach your Energy at the end of the turn, not the start. Don’t bench a Pokémon until you need it — on the Bench it’s a target, in your hand it’s information your opponent doesn’t have.
  • Disrupt before you reveal. If you’re playing something that forces your opponent to make a choice, play it before you show them your full board, so they have to choose blind.

The habit to build: before each card, ask “does playing this tell me something I don’t know yet, or does it lock me in?” Do the first kind first.

Your first tournament

If you’re heading to a league night or a local event, a few things catch people out the first time:

  • Deck list. You write down all 60 cards and hand it in before you play. It stops anyone swapping decks mid-event, and once it’s submitted, that’s your deck for the day.
  • Deck check. Judges can pull your deck and count it against your list. Your list has to match what’s in your hands — a mismatch is where penalties come from, and they range from a warning up to a game loss depending on how serious it is.
  • Sleeves. Every card in the deck needs identical sleeves, in good condition. Scuffed, bent or otherwise distinguishable sleeves can be treated as marked cards, which is taken seriously because it looks like cheating whether or not you meant it. Bring a spare pack.
  • Shuffling and cutting. Shuffle properly, then offer your deck to your opponent to cut. Do it every time. It costs you nothing and it’s the norm.
  • Check your own legality. Nobody else is responsible for your deck being format-legal. Check the regulation marks yourself before you go — see the rotation section above.

Beyond that, ask. Judges would far rather answer a question than issue a penalty, and every player at a local event was new once.

Where to go from here

Have a look at Meta Decks for what’s actually winning right now, or Jack’s Decks for what I play. If you want a game — in person in Singapore or on Pokémon TCG Live — that’s Play with Jack. And if you’d rather learn in a room full of people who play, BlackLabel TCG runs Gym nights.

Work With Me

For shops, brands, organisers, and anyone else who makes things happen in the Pokémon world.

Who I am

I’m Jackson — Singaporean, a dad, an operations manager by day, a singer-songwriter the rest of the time, and a Pokémon TCG obsessive for as long as I can remember. ItemSixHQ is where all of that meets.

I run this alone, at night, after my kid’s asleep. Nobody pays me to. Everything on this site — the guides, the news write-ups, the card photography, the site itself — exists because I wanted it to exist and nobody else had made it.

What I actually care about

There are a lot of people selling Pokémon cards. There are fewer trying to make the hobby easier to get into, and fewer still willing to talk anyone out of a purchase.

My whole approach comes down to a few things I won’t bend on:

  • Honesty over margin. I price low on purpose. I write condition notes that lose me money. I’ve told people not to buy a card because it wasn’t what they wanted.
  • The hobby isn’t an asset class. I’m not here to help anyone flip cards. I’m here for the people who want the card because they want the card.
  • Teaching is the point. The guides on this site are free, fact-checked against official rulings, and written for someone who knows nothing. That’s the part I’m proudest of.
  • Credit where it’s due. I run an unpaid page recommending someone else’s shop because the community there is genuinely good. That’s not a strategy, it’s just correct.

What I’m building toward

The Pokémon World Championships come to Singapore in August 2027. It’s the first time the event has been anywhere near my home, and realistically it’s a once-in-a-lifetime thing for a Singaporean fan.

Between now and then I want to be genuinely useful to the people coming — players, families, visitors who’ve never been to Singapore before. I’m building the Worlds 2027 hub for exactly that, and it’ll keep growing as real information gets announced.

Beyond that: more written guides, getting the video side of ItemSixHQ properly going again, and running things locally that get new people playing rather than just buying.

What I’m open to

  • Sponsorship or product support — sleeves, storage, playmats, deck boxes, anything a player actually touches. I’ll say honestly what I think of it, which is the only reason my saying anything is worth having.
  • Event coverage — locals, regionals, Worlds 2027 itself. Written, filmed, or both.
  • Collaborations with shops and communities — beginner nights, learn-to-play sessions, guides written for your players.
  • Media, press and creator passes — particularly anything Worlds 2027 related.
  • Writing for other people — if you need someone who can explain this game clearly, I can do that.

What I’m not after: anything that needs me to pretend. No paid positive reviews, no promoting things I haven’t used, nothing that treats the hobby as an investment vehicle. If a partnership needs me to be less honest, it’s not worth it to me.

Press, media and event coverage

If you’re assessing me for a media or creator pass, this section is for you.

What I publish. Written guides and rules explainers, a free deck-legality tool, news write-ups in my own words, and a running visitor guide to Worlds 2027 in Singapore. Everything on this site is free, and none of it is behind a sign-up.

Who I write for. Players in Singapore and Southeast Asia, and beginners anywhere. English-language coverage of this game is overwhelmingly North American, and a player here reads guides with the wrong currency, the wrong shops and the wrong release calendar. That gap is the entire reason this site exists.

What I’d cover at an event. Written coverage aimed at first-time attendees and at regional players — how to actually navigate the event, what the format looked like, who from this part of the world made a run at it, and what a newcomer should take away from it. Filmed coverage as well, where that makes sense.

Where I am honestly. I’m not going to dress this up. My long-form videos sit in the 2,000–3,500 view range and short-form has reached about 7,000. That’s a small audience and I’d rather tell you the real number than a flattering one.

What I’d point at instead is the work. The guides on this site are written and fact-checked against official rulings, the rotation checker is a tool nobody else in this region maintains, and the Worlds 2027 hub is being built ten months ahead of the event. That’s the standard I hold, and the audience is the part I’m still building.

Live, three nights a week. I stream on Twitch every Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. Tuesdays are Pokémon — TCG Live, the video games, and whatever is happening in the game that week. Wednesdays are open. Thursdays I play and sing. It averages around 20 concurrent viewers — a small room, but a consistent one, and across a three-hour stream that’s roughly 60 viewer-hours of people who chose to stay rather than scroll past.

What I’m Hunting

The other half of a binder. If you have any of this and want something of mine, let’s talk.

Everyone puts up what they’re getting rid of. Far fewer people say what they actually want, which is strange, because that’s the half that makes a trade happen.

So: here’s what I’m after. If you’ve got something on this list, look through the binder and tell me what you’d want for it. I’ll be straightforward about whether it works — and if I think you’re giving up too much, I’ll say that too.

Always interested

  • Japanese printsstanding Particularly older Gym-era cards. Better print quality, better art, and the part of the hobby I enjoy most.
  • Cards with a clean swirlstanding The little galaxy in the foil. I like them for what they are, not for a premium — and I’ll tell you honestly if I don’t think yours carries one.
  • Bulk commons and uncommonsgiving away Not for the binder. These go straight to people learning the game — see Giving Back. If you’re about to bin a shoebox of these, send them here instead.
  • Playable Standard staplesfor decks Search cards, draw supporters, anything on a current regulation mark. Condition matters much less to me here — played is fine if it shuffles.

Specific cards I’m chasing

    How a trade works with me

    • Value both sides openly. Every card in my binder has a number on it taken from what copies have actually sold for. Do the same on your side and we’ll both know quickly whether it’s fair.
    • Uneven is fine. If one side is short, we settle the difference in cash either way, or you throw in something small. No drama.
    • Condition gets stated up front. Mine are written on every listing. I’d ask the same of you — a photo in decent light saves us both a conversation.
    • I’ll talk you out of a bad one. If you’re handing over more than you should, I’m going to point it out. That has cost me trades and I’d do it again.

    Singapore only for now, same as everything else — meet-ups or local mail.

    Learn the Pokémon TCG

    Everything I’ve written about actually playing this game, in the order I’d hand it to a friend. All free, all fact-checked, none of it behind anything.

    I started writing these because the explanations I could find were either three minutes long and useless, or forty minutes long and assumed you already knew what a Prize card was. This is my attempt at the middle.

    Start here Beginners Guide What’s in a deck, how a turn works, how you actually win.     Rotation Checker

    Paste a decklist. I’ll tell you what’s Standard-legal today, what rotates next, and what’s already out.

    Every card printed since 2023 has a small letter in a black box near the bottom edge — the regulation mark. Standard legality is decided entirely by that letter, not by how new the card looks or how much it cost.

    Right now, these are the marks that are legal:

    How to read the result

    • Legal — fine to play in Standard today, and not first in line to rotate.
    • Rotates next — legal right now, but it’s the oldest mark still standing. When the next rotation happens, this is what goes. Don’t build a new deck around these if you’re planning to play competitively for the next year.
    • Not legal — already rotated out of Standard. Still perfectly good for Expanded, for casual games, and for your binder.
    • Check the card — promos and a few odd printings don’t share one mark across the whole set. Look at the actual card in your hand.

    The bit I have to say out loud

    This is a tool I maintain by hand, on a website I run at night. It is not official, it is not affiliated with Pokémon, and it can be out of date — particularly in the few weeks after a new set lands.

    If you are travelling to a tournament, check the official Play! Pokémon rules and formats page before you go. Use this to catch problems early, not to settle an argument at a judge’s table.

    One more thing it can’t do: it reads set codes, not individual cards. If a specific card has been banned on its own, or a printing carries a different mark to the rest of its set, this won’t know. It also doesn’t check the one-ACE-SPEC-per-deck rule.

    Ask Jack

    The questions I get asked most, answered the way I’d answer them in person — including the ones where the honest answer costs me a sale.

    People message me on Telegram with the same handful of questions, so I’ve started writing the answers down here. Nothing is behind a form and I’m not collecting anything — if you’ve got a question that isn’t here, just message me and if it’s a good one it’ll end up on this page.

    Cards you already own

    I found my old cards from the 90s. Am I sitting on money?

    Almost certainly not, and I’d rather tell you that now than let you spend a weekend hoping.

    The vast majority of cards from any era are worth well under a dollar. What carries value is a short list: first edition and shadowless Base Set, a handful of specific holos in genuinely clean condition, sealed product, and a few promos. Condition matters more than age — a played Base Set Charizard with white edges and a soft crease is a different object entirely from a clean one.

    Check a few against recent sold listings, not asking prices. Asking prices are fiction. And if the whole binder comes to twenty dollars, that’s a normal, common outcome, not a sign you did something wrong.

    Should I get my card graded?

    Usually no. Grading costs money per card plus shipping and insurance, and it takes months. For that to make sense, the graded card has to be worth meaningfully more than the raw one plus the fee — and for most cards it simply isn’t.

    It’s worth considering when the card is already worth a few hundred raw, when it looks close to flawless under a light, or when it’s something you want to keep forever and the slab is really about protection and provenance.

    I won’t predict what grade something will get. I’m not a grader, and people who guess grades for other people are usually about to sell them something.

    How do I know if a card is fake?

    Feel it first. Real cards have a specific stiffness and a faint texture; most counterfeits are either too floppy or too glossy. Then look at the back — the blue is a very particular shade and fakes are usually too dark, too purple, or too washed out.

    After that: the text should be crisp under a phone camera zoom, not fuzzy at the edges. The energy symbols should be sharp. Check the set code and card number against a database and make sure that card actually exists at that number in that set.

    If you have a real card of the same era, compare them side by side. That single trick catches more fakes than any checklist.

    What’s a “swirl” and does it make my card worth more?

    A swirl is a pattern in the holo foil, caused during manufacturing, that looks like a little galaxy or fingerprint in the shine. Collectors like them because every one is unique.

    Does it add value? Sometimes, on the right card, to the right buyer. On most cards it adds nothing you could reliably sell for. I’ve looked at comparable sales for swirled cards in my own binder and priced several of them at exactly the same number as an unswirled copy, because that’s what the actual sold listings said.

    Buying and collecting

    Are booster boxes a good investment?

    I’m going to be unhelpful here on purpose: I don’t think of cards as an investment, and I’m not going to help anyone treat them as one.

    What I can tell you factually is that sealed product is printed in enormous quantities now, far more than in the 90s, and that most modern sets stay near or below retail for a long time. People who did well out of sealed product mostly did well out of a specific set at a specific moment, and that’s not a strategy, it’s hindsight.

    Buy a box because opening it looks fun. If it goes up, nice. If you need it to go up, buy something else.

    Should I buy Japanese cards or English?

    Japanese cards are generally better made — better centring, more consistent print quality — and often cheaper, because Japanese sets are smaller and the pull rates are kinder. If you’re collecting for the art, Japanese is frequently the better buy.

    If you want to play in an English-language tournament, you need English cards. Mixed-language decks generally aren’t allowed in official play, so buy for the purpose you actually have.

    My kid wants to start. What do I actually buy?

    Two pre-built theme decks, or one Battle Academy style box, and nothing else. Around thirty or forty dollars total. They can play each other immediately, out of the box, without you having to understand deckbuilding.

    Do not start with booster packs. Packs are a lottery, not a way to build something playable, and a child who opens ten packs still can’t play a game with what’s inside.

    Then let them play for a few weeks before spending anything else. Most of the enjoyment is in the playing, and you’ll find out quickly whether it stuck.

    Do I need to sleeve and toploader everything?

    No. Sleeve what you play with, because shuffling is what actually wears a card. Sleeve and protect the small number of cards that are genuinely worth something. Everything else can live happily in a binder.

    The most common mistake I see is spending more on protection than the cards are worth. The second most common is using cheap PVC pages that damage cards over years — if you buy one thing, make it acid-free, PVC-free binder pages.

    Playing

    I want to actually play. Where do I start?

    Read the Beginners Guide on this site, then download Pokémon TCG Live and play the tutorial. It’s free, it enforces the rules for you, and you can lose in private for a week without anyone watching.

    After that, find a local league night. In Singapore there are shops running them regularly — BlackLabel TCG is one I recommend and have no arrangement with. Bring whatever deck you have. Everyone there was new once and most of them will happily help you fix your list.

    Or message me and I’ll play you. I don’t mind losing and I definitely don’t mind explaining.

    Why did my deck stop being legal?

    Rotation. Once a year, the oldest cards drop out of the Standard format, and they drop out by regulation mark — the little letter in a box near the bottom of the card.

    The confusing part is that it’s per printing, not per card name. If a card you own got reprinted in a newer set with a newer mark, the new copy is legal and yours still isn’t. Same artwork, same name, different legality.

    Paste your list into the Rotation Checker and it’ll show you exactly which lines are the problem.

    What’s the cheapest way to build a deck that can actually win?

    Pick one archetype and buy only for it. The expensive mistake is buying singles for three decks at once and finishing none of them.

    Most of a competitive deck’s cost is a handful of cards. The trainers — the search cards, the draw supporters — are usually cheap and get reused across everything you build, so buying those first is never wasted money.

    And check what rotates before you spend. Building a deck around cards with the oldest legal mark is the single most common way new players waste money.

    About this site

    Why are your prices lower than everywhere else?

    Because this isn’t how I pay rent. I have a day job. The cards are from my own binder, I price them off actual sold listings rather than what I’d like them to be worth, and I’d rather a card went to someone who wanted it than sat here at a number nobody will pay.

    The trade-off is that I’m slow, I only ship within Singapore, and there’s no shop infrastructure behind any of this. If you need something urgently, a real shop is a better bet and I’ll say so.

    Can you hold a card for me?

    Honestly, no. I’ve been burned by it enough times that I stopped. If you’re ready, message me and we’ll sort it out the same week — that’s genuinely as fast as I can be, and it’s fast enough.

    Ask me something

    There’s no form here on purpose — this site collects nothing about you and I’d like to keep it that way. Telegram or Discord both reach me. I answer everything that isn’t spam, usually within a day or two.

    Worlds 2027, Singapore

    The Pokémon World Championships are coming to my home city. This page is my running guide for anyone travelling in for it — and it’ll keep growing as real details get announced.

    What’s confirmed

    Dates
    13–15 August 2027. Announced by Pokémon at the closing ceremony of Worlds 2026 in San Francisco, on 30 August 2026.
    City
    Singapore. Only the fourth time Worlds has been held outside the United States — after Canada in 2013, the UK in 2022, and Japan in 2023.

    What’s reported but not official yet

    Singapore press covering the announcement reported the venue as Singapore EXPO, with Championship Sunday at the Singapore Indoor Stadium. That came from Pokémon’s own social posts rather than a formal venue announcement, so treat it as very likely but not yet locked.

    I’ll update this the moment there’s an official confirmation, and I’ll say plainly when I do.

    What nobody knows yet

    • Tickets. No dates, no prices, no idea yet whether spectator passes work the way they did in San Francisco.
    • Qualification. How Championship Points and invites work for the 2027 season hasn’t been laid out.
    • Side events and schedule. Nothing announced.
    • Whether there’s a PokémonXP convention alongside it. Those only happen in select years, and none was announced for 2027.

    If you see any of the above stated confidently somewhere else right now, it’s a guess.

    If you’re flying in — Singapore basics

    This part I can help with now, because it doesn’t depend on any announcement.

    • August weather. Hot and humid, roughly 26–32°C, with sudden heavy downpours that stop as fast as they start. Bring a light rain layer, not a coat. Everything indoors is aggressively air-conditioned, so a light long-sleeve for inside is genuinely sensible.
    • Getting around. The MRT is clean, cheap and goes almost everywhere. You can tap in with a contactless bank card or your phone — no need to buy a transit card.
    • Language. English is an official language and is what you’ll be spoken to in. You do not need to prepare anything.
    • Cards and cash. Cards are accepted nearly everywhere. Local payments run on PayNow, which needs a Singapore bank account — so carry a bit of cash for hawker centres and smaller shops.
    • Food. Eat at hawker centres. It’s the best food in the country and it’s cheap. This is the single most common thing visitors get wrong.

    I’ll add proper venue-area recommendations — food, hotels, where to get singles, where people actually play — once the venue is officially confirmed and I know which part of the island to point you at.

    Where to play while you’re here

    Singapore has a small but genuinely welcoming TCG scene. If you want a game outside the tournament, the friendliest starting point I know is BlackLabel TCG — a shop I have no affiliation with, run by a friend, with official Gym nights on Fridays and Saturdays.

    And if you want a game with me specifically: that’s here. I’ll happily meet a visitor for a match and point you at good food afterwards.

    My own plan

    I want to be there — as a competitor, as a creator covering it, or both. I’ve written about that properly, and this hub is part of the same effort: be useful to people coming to my city, starting well before anyone asks.

    If you organise, cover or sponsor anything in this space, here’s what I’m about.

    Terms & Conditions

    Read this first — it’ll save us both time

    I’m not a shop. I’m a hobbyist with a day job and a toddler, selling out of my own binder to other people who love these cards. Everything here is priced to be fair, not to make me money — the margin is deliberately thin, because the point is getting cards into the hands of people who’ll enjoy them.

    That’s also why I’m upfront about what I can’t do. I’m one person doing this around a full-time job, so there are a few things I’ll usually say no to:

    • “Can you send more photos / close-ups of the edges?” For most cards, no. Photographing and re-photographing individual cards for every enquiry isn’t something I have hours for. What’s written in the listing is what I’ve got.
    • “Do you think this would grade a 9 or a 10?” I genuinely don’t know, and I’d rather not guess. I’m not a grader, and a guess from me isn’t worth anything to you.
    • “Can you hold this while I decide?” Usually not for long. I’m not running a reservation system out of my phone.

    So if I take a while to reply, or don’t reply at all, it’s almost always one of those three — or simply that I’m at work or putting my kid to bed. It’s never personal, and it’s not me ignoring you because your order is small. Small orders are completely welcome.

    The one rule of thumb that matters: if you’re unsure, assume every card is binder condition and assume nothing would grade a 10. If you’re buying to flip or to grade, I’m probably not the seller you want — and that’s fine, no hard feelings either way.

    But if you’re after a card because you actually want the card? That’s exactly who this is for. Ask away, and I’ll help however I can.

    Right — on with the actual terms. Kthxbye!

    The short version: this is a personal binder, not a store. Here’s exactly how it works.

    No direct purchasing

    This website has no direct purchasing capability — and that’s not a flaw, it’s designed this way on purpose. It’s a digital binder: a way to see what Jack currently has, so you can message him about anything you’re interested in. There’s no shop, no checkout, and no automated anything — every sale is arranged directly between you and Jack, one conversation at a time.

    How to trade or buy something

    Found something you want? Click “Add to my trade list” on the listing. Once you’re done browsing, open My Trade List and select “Send Jack this list.” You can contact Jack via Telegram DMs, or by joining his Discord server and either DM-ing him privately or asking in the Pokémon text channel.

    Once your message comes through, Jack will respond as soon as he can. Trades are genuinely welcome — if you’d rather swap cards than pay for them, say so and he’ll tell you honestly whether it works for him. Have a look at what he’s hunting first.

    If you’re buying rather than trading, payment is made via PayNow or PayLah! — Jack will send over a QR code along with your final order amount and item list before you pay.

    Jack has a day job and a young kid at home, so please be a little forgiving if he takes a bit longer than usual to reply — he’ll always get back to you.

    Collection & mailing

    Jack is based in Singapore, and can only hand over cards locally — there’s no international shipping at the moment. Once payment is confirmed, cards can be collected in person or mailed out:

    • Tampines MRT — specific days and timings only, DM Jack to discuss.
    • Upper Thomson MRT — Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, 2–7pm.
    • Mailing (SmartPac) — available for an additional $3. Multiple cards can share one SmartPac unless the order is too large.

    Sending your list

    Your whole list, and its links, is copied automatically when you hit “Send Jack this list” — simply paste it into the chat and he’ll respond as soon as he can.

    Condition guide

    Every card is graded honestly on this scale. Anything Moderately Played or below gets a written note under the listing explaining exactly where and how it’s worn.

    M
    Mint — flawless, pack-fresh.
    NM
    Near Mint — minimal to no wear.
    LP
    Lightly Played — minor edge/corner wear.
    MP
    Moderately Played — visible scratches or whitening.
    HP
    Heavily Played — heavy wear, possible small tears.
    DMG
    Damaged — bends, tears, writing, or similar.

    Card flags explained

    Some listings carry small badges for printing quirks that collectors look for. They’re not damage — they describe how the card came out of the factory.

    Swirls
    A galaxy-like swirl pattern in the holo foil, created during printing. Often sought after.
    Holo Bleed
    Holo foil extending slightly past the artwork window onto the border. A printing quirk some collectors prize.
    Misprint
    A factory error — miscut edges, off-centre printing, or ink irregularities.

    About the photos

    Thumbnail photos on this site are not an actual photo of the specific physical card and don’t represent its real condition. Please trust the condition, remarks, and any flags (swirls, holo bleed, misprint) stated on each individual listing. If you’d like real photos or more explanation about a specific card before committing, just message Jack — he’s happy to help.

    Authenticity & sales

    Everything in the binder is genuine, official Pokémon TCG product. No counterfeits, no reprints passed off as originals, no bootlegs — if it’s listed as a real card, it is one.

    If I ever list anything that isn’t official product — a custom, a fan-made card, a playtest proxy, something a friend designed — it will say so plainly in the listing name and the remarks, and it will never be priced or described as the real thing. You will always know which one you’re buying.

    All sales are final once you’ve collected or received the item, so please double-check it against the listed condition, remarks, and flags before paying. If something arrives clearly different from what was listed (wrong card, or condition way off from what was described), message Jack and he’ll sort it out — but a change of mind isn’t grounds for a refund.
